title: Philippine Immigration Detention: If You Don't Pay, Your Deportation Never Moves
dek: A Chinese surfer was locked up in the Philippines for 41 days. What he saw wasn't a prison — it was a business with a price list: beds, boxed meals, phones, lawyer fees, everything had to be bought. Those who didn't pay were held for years, even over a decade.
why: StoryFM's Behind Bars series. Medium information density but solid detail. The first half is a personal ordeal; the second half — the gang economy inside the detention center, the ransom quotes from scam companies, the lawyers jacking up prices on the spot — is the part that's actually worth something.
who: Founders and overseas-expansion practitioners interested in the situation of Chinese abroad, the Philippine business environment, and the gray-industry and immigration-corruption machinery.
skip: 6:29-9:14 — surfing experience and startup background, unrelated to the core mechanism.

points.h: Immigration offered to release him on the spot for 1.5 million pesos
points.body: The night Feili was arrested, immigration officers pulled him aside and whispered, "I can help you." After talking to a lawyer, the feedback was: pay 1.5 million pesos, about 160,000-170,000 RMB, and you can walk immediately, no problem at all. Of the 12 to 13 people arrested in the same batch, no one agreed to pay. Everyone thought it was impossible that such a thing could still exist in 2026 and wanted to resolve it through normal legal procedures. But the price of refusal was this: they were transferred from the holding cell at the General City police station to the detention center at the Bureau of Immigration headquarters in Manila, where Feili ultimately spent 41 days.

points.h: When his phone was confiscated, money in Gcash was transferred out
points.body: When Feili was detained, his phone was taken. They asked for his unlock code, and he thought it was normal procedure so he gave it. His phone unlock code was the same as his Gcash payment password. For the next four or five days, no matter how he applied, he couldn't get the phone back — until he kept pressuring the Chinese consulate and a lawyer, and the phone was finally returned. When he turned it on, the interface was all in English, and the Gcash transfer records showed money had been sent out, but it had been transferred back the night before he got the phone. There was only about 1,000 RMB in it. Feili said it wasn't about the amount — it was that the phone had been tampered with while it wasn't in his hands. He reasoned that many Chinese doing gray-industry scams in Manila who get arrested go through this same layer of fleecing, but they don't dare go to the Chinese consulate because their phones contain a mass of criminal evidence.

points.h: The air conditioning and takeout the immigration bureau promised were another form
points.body: For those unwilling to buy their own plane ticket to transfer, the immigration bureau would take turns working on them, saying the Manila immigration facilities were very good, had air conditioning, were very free — you could work out, play basketball, order takeout, use your phone. Feili said they weren't lying: there really was air conditioning, you really could order takeout — it was just another form, a completely different form. They arrived at the headquarters detention center at past 3 a.m. After getting off the vehicle, what he saw was a square area, an outer layer of iron grating, a tin roof above, iron cages like dog kennels all around, and inside, long communal sleeping platforms with several hundred people. At past 3 a.m., many people weren't sleeping — bare-chested, wearing only underwear, clinging to the iron cages to look at the newcomers. Feili said he and the other foreigners didn't say a word for several minutes after getting off, then it hit them: they'd been lied to by the immigration bureau.

points.h: The detention center is a business invested in by a Chinese boss
points.body: What Feili heard inside was that this immigration detention center was invested in by a Chinese boss, in cooperation with the immigration bureau, and the beds, toilets and other facilities were newly built by the Chinese boss. Foreigners could stay as they were, but Chinese who came in had to pay. The lowest-tier communal bed was 10,000 pesos a month, about 1,100-1,200 RMB. Wealthy "pan zong" bosses and gambling big shots could pay 50,000 pesos a month, about 6,000-plus RMB, for a so-called "air-conditioned room" — actually the bed was the same, just wrapped in tin foil and wooden boards, with a foam box of ice beside it, a hole cut in the box, and an exhaust fan drawing the cold air into the bed. That's where the immigration bureau's earlier claim of "there's air conditioning inside" came from.

points.h: Chinese gangs collect protection money: you don't want to pay but still want to get out?
points.body: On Feili's first day inside, the head of the Chinese gang came to him for the "rumor fee," saying the facilities were all their investment and it was impossible to stay for free. Feili said he had no money, he was here to serve time, how could he have to pay on top of that. The gang boss said with a threatening tone: you're already in here, you don't want to spend money and you still think you're getting out? Feili learned that it was managed by gangs inside, and the Chinese gang monopolized all food, clothing and daily life for Chinese — running a Chinese restaurant and a Chinese supermarket. The whole detention center held about 200 people; when Feili went in it was the off-season, and Chinese numbered over 100, with gambling and gray industry making up more than half. The Chinese gang's employees were paid wages — the head chef 10,000 pesos a month, the assistant cook 5,000 pesos — very low wages, but many people couldn't get out because they had no money for a lawyer and could only work to earn money.

points.h: A Yunnan man held for over a year; his family thought he died in Southeast Asia
points.body: A man from Yunnan asked Feili for help. Before the pandemic, he'd been lured to the Philippines by a high-salary recruitment ad; the moment he landed, his phone and passport were taken, and he was pulled into a park to do telecom fraud. When his performance was poor, the supervisor shocked him with an electric baton every day. After the company was busted, he served a few months, then was transferred to the immigration detention center. The normal deportation procedure is simple — a few departments sign, you buy your own ticket, and you can go — but the immigration bureau, in order to make money, will hold you for a very long time; if you don't pay, the procedure won't move. He'd already been held for over a year, had not a cent, no phone, could only eat prison food every day, couldn't reach his family, and his family thought he'd died in Southeast Asia. Feili helped him write a Chinese letter and translate it into English, and through an introduction by a Japanese uncle, got to see the warden. The warden had a guard bring Feili's phone, and had Xiaopang add his father on WeChat and send a selfie and a voice message. Afterwards, the immigration bureau bought a basic phone specifically to solve this problem.

points.h: Scam company ransom: 3 million pesos per person
points.body: The only Chinese person Feili talked with much was from a scam company. The company's 70 or 80 people were surrounded by the immigration bureau together with the police and the NBI, three agencies. The first wave of fleecing was the NBI and police locking each person in a toilet — because there were no cameras in the toilets — and taking everything valuable off them. The second wave was the immigration bureau negotiating with the company boss for ransom: the quote per person varied — 1 million, 2 million, 3 million pesos — depending on the person in charge's mood. That company negotiated at 3 million pesos per person, about 300,000-plus RMB. The boss ultimately ransomed 30 people, exactly the 30 held on one floor; the rest were promised food deliveries until they got out. This young man worked a book targeting the Japanese market, scamming middle-aged Japanese women. In his best month he made 2 million RMB, bought a house and a car in his small hometown county. Later he was kidnapped by a friend, had several hundred thousand transferred away, and was framed by a corrupt cop with an illegal gun possession charge, so he couldn't leave.

points.h: A Philippine lawyer raised the price on the spot when he saw he was Chinese
points.body: In Cebu, Feili was introduced by a Lithuanian to a Philippine lawyer, quoted at 200,000 pesos, about 20,000-plus RMB, done in four weeks. After arriving in Manila, the lawyer came to visit, saw he was Chinese, and immediately raised the price, saying that was the old price and the new price required an additional 120,000 pesos, about 10,000-plus RMB. Feili decided not to use him and forfeited the deposit, turning instead to a Chinese middleman. The Chinese middleman quoted 30,000-plus RMB, four to six weeks, no more than six weeks. Feili said the truly reliable Chinese middlemen know this procedure inside out, because everyone locked up inside is Chinese. In the end he was held inside for over 30 days, plus Cebu, 41 days total. The Lithuanian who introduced the Philippine lawyer — when Feili messaged him, he still hadn't gotten out.

quotes.text: If you give him 1.5 million pesos now, he can release you immediately, and you'll have no problem at all.
But it's not about the amount of money — when the phone wasn't in my hands, money was transferred out.

Look at his corrupt bureaucratic system and his ordinary people as separate things. I still believe Filipinos are fundamentally very good people, but the bureaucratic system is truly too corrupt — and it's the kind that drinks blood, drinks human blood.
